rows.summary: This document explains methods for accessing the Kubernetes API from within a Pod, focusing on using official client libraries and directly accessing the REST API with service account credentials.
This document explains the steps required to add Windows worker nodes to an existing kubeadm cluster. It details the process of installing containerd, kubeadm, and kubelet, and joining the cluster.

This document explains how to specify CPU and memory resources for a Pod at the pod-level, detailing precedence rules and limitations. It guides users on enabling necessary feature gates and creating pods with pod-level resource specifications.

This document explains how to enable and configure automatic certificate rotation for the kubelet. It details the flags and processes involved in the kubelet requesting and using new certificates from the Kubernetes API.

This document provides the operational steps to migrate a node's container runtime from Docker Engine to containerd. It details the process of draining the node, installing containerd, and configuring the kubelet to use it.

This document explains how to use a shared Volume to enable communication between two containers running within the same Kubernetes Pod. It demonstrates creating a Pod with an Nginx container and a Debian container that write data to be served by Nginx.

This document explains how to enable or disable feature gates in a Kubernetes cluster to control specific features. It details configuration steps during cluster initialization and on existing clusters.

This document explains how to use ConfigMaps in Kubernetes to inject configuration data into application pods. It details various methods for creating ConfigMaps from directories, files, and literal values.

This document explains the operational expectations, resource requirements, and tools needed for managing etcd clusters in a Kubernetes environment. It covers starting, securing, backing up, and scaling these distributed systems.

This document explains how to configure default CPU requests and limits for a Kubernetes namespace using a LimitRange. It details the process of creating a namespace, applying a LimitRange, and observing how default values are applied to Pods.

This document explains how to use `crictl`, a command-line interface for CRI-compatible container runtimes, to inspect and debug containers on a Kubernetes node. It covers installation, general usage, and examples of commands.

This guide provides steps to help users debug applications deployed in Kubernetes that are not behaving correctly. It covers diagnosing issues related to Pod states like pending, waiting, and terminating.

This document explains how to use the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API to declare network policies governing pod communication. It provides steps to create a deployment, expose it, and apply a network policy.

This document explains how to define dependent environment variables for containers within a Kubernetes Pod using the $(VAR_NAME) syntax. It details how references are resolved and the importance of the order of environment variables.
This document provides hints for diagnosing DNS resolution problems within a cluster. It guides users through creating test pods and checking local configurations to identify issues with CoreDNS.

This document explains how to configure the built-in Kubernetes Admission Controller to enforce Pod Security Standards. It details the YAML configuration required to set cluster-wide defaults and exemptions.
This document explains how to assign extended resources to a container within a Kubernetes Pod manifest. It demonstrates requesting resources and how scheduling fails when capacity is insufficient.

This document guides cluster administrators on hardening authorization for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) by implementing least-privilege permissions for status updates. It details how to grant specific permissions to different DRA components.

This document explains how to use `kubectl` with YAML or JSON configuration files to create, update, delete, and view Kubernetes objects. It discusses the trade-offs between imperative commands and declarative configuration.
This guide explains how to configure and enable the `ip-masq-agent`. It details how the agent configures iptables rules to hide pod IP addresses behind the node's IP address for external traffic.

This document explains how to use the `kubectl debug node` command to deploy an interactive Pod on a specific Kubernetes Node for troubleshooting. It details how to access host filesystem logs and important considerations when using debugging Pods.

This document explains how to use Kustomize to declaratively customize Kubernetes objects. It details features like generating resources from files and composing and customizing collections of resources.
This document explains how to create, edit, and manage Kubernetes Secret objects using the kubectl command-line tool. It details methods for providing secret data via raw literals or source files.

This document explains how to configure default memory requests and limits for a Kubernetes namespace using a LimitRange. It details the steps to create a namespace, apply a LimitRange, and how default values are applied to Pods.

This document explains how to use the Node Problem Detector daemon to monitor node health. It details methods for enabling the detector using kubectl, Addon pods, and overwriting the default configuration.

This document explains how to configure a DaemonSet to run its pods only on nodes that have local SSD storage. It details the steps of labeling nodes, creating a manifest with a node selector, and deploying the DaemonSet.

This document explains how to set a quota for the total number of Pods allowed in a Kubernetes Namespace using a ResourceQuota object. It provides steps for creating the namespace, applying the quota, and observing how it limits deployments.
This document provides the steps necessary to perform a rollback on a Kubernetes DaemonSet. It explains how to find revisions, execute the rollback command, and monitor the progress.

This document provides recommendations for protecting a Kubernetes cluster from accidental or malicious access. It details security measures for API access, authentication, authorization, and protecting cluster components.

This document explains how to use an SSH client to create a SOCKS5 proxy tunnel to access a remote Kubernetes API server. It details the SSH command and how to configure kubectl to use the created proxy.

This document outlines best practices for designing and implementing admission webhooks in Kubernetes. It covers considerations for performance, preventing loops, managing scope, and ensuring idempotence.
The aggregation layer extends Kubernetes with additional APIs beyond the core set. It functions by proxying requests to registered APIServices, allowing for custom API extensions.
This document explains cgroup v2, the next generation of the Linux cgroup API. It details its unified hierarchy, enhanced resource management capabilities, and the requirements for its use.

This document explains a common set of recommended labels for Kubernetes objects to enable interoperability and queryability. These labels help describe applications and their components in a standardized manner.
This document explains the concepts of containers, container images, and container runtimes. It details how containers decouple applications from infrastructure and the principles of immutability.
This document explains what a CronJob is, how it creates scheduled Jobs, and the syntax used to define the recurring schedule. It details the structure of a CronJob specification and its limitations.
This document explains the types of disruptions that can affect Pods, categorizing them as voluntary or involuntary. It also provides mitigation strategies for dealing with involuntary disruptions.
This document explains how to observe the status and health of resources dynamically allocated with DRA. It details methods like kubelet metrics and driver-reported device status.

This document explains ephemeral containers, which are temporary containers run inside an existing Pod for user-initiated actions like troubleshooting. They are not suitable for building applications.

Finalizers control the garbage collection of objects by alerting controllers to perform specific cleanup tasks before deletion. They work by preventing resource removal until all specified finalizer conditions are satisfied.

This document explains what a container image is, how they are named (using tags and digests), and how Kubernetes references them. It covers concepts like image naming conventions and registry interactions.

This document explains how to expose the state of Kubernetes objects as metrics using kube-state-metrics. It details how these metrics can be queried and used for alerting within a monitoring system like Prometheus.

This document describes security features in the Linux kernel that can be leveraged within Kubernetes Pods and containers. It explains how to use features like seccomp, AppArmor, and SELinux to enhance workload isolation and security.

This document provides an overview of configuration options and best practices for cluster multi-tenancy. It discusses different sharing models like multi-team and multi-customer tenancy in Kubernetes.

topics: Node constraints imposed by autoscaler configuration
rows.summary: This document explains how nodes in a cluster can be dynamically provisioned or consolidated to provide necessary capacity while optimizing costs. It details the mechanisms and constraints involved in node autoscaling.

This document overviews the different techniques for creating and managing Kubernetes objects using the `kubectl` command-line tool. It details imperative commands, imperative object configuration, and declarative object configuration.

This document provides an overview of Kubernetes, explaining what it is, its origins, and why it is necessary for managing containerized, distributed systems. It details the core capabilities Kubernetes offers for resilience and deployment.

This document explains Kubernetes Pod conditions, which are markers indicating specific aspects of a Pod's actual state. Conditions complement the Pod's phase by tracking multiple independent states like container readiness or resize operations.

This document introduces Kubernetes Quality of Service (QoS) classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort. It explains how these classes are assigned based on resource requests and limits to influence how Kubernetes handles Pod eviction during node pressure.

This document explains the PodGroup scheduling mechanism, which evaluates a group of Pods as a single unit to prevent resource deadlocks. It details the PodGroup scheduling cycle and the algorithms used for placement and selection.
This document explains the various types of proxies used within a Kubernetes environment, detailing their function and how they interact with the API server and services.

This document explains resource bin packing in the context of scheduling a single pod. It details two scoring strategies, MostAllocated and RequestedToCapacityRatio, used by the kube-scheduler to decide where to place pods.

RuntimeClass is a feature for selecting the container runtime configuration used to run Pod containers. It allows balancing performance and security by specifying different runtime settings for different workloads.

The Scheduling Framework is a pluggable architecture for the Kubernetes scheduler, allowing scheduling features to be implemented as plugins. It defines a workflow involving scheduling and binding cycles to determine Pod placement.

This document explains how Kubernetes automatically maintains workload health and availability through self-healing mechanisms. It details features like container restarts, replica replacement, and persistent storage recovery.

This document explains Static Pods, which are managed directly by the kubelet on a node without API server observation. It details their use for self-hosted control planes and contrasts them with DaemonSets.

This document explains the concept of storage versions in Kubernetes, detailing how objects are serialized in the backing store and how the API server handles conversions between API representations and stored encodings.

This document explains how Kubernetes system components emit traces using the OpenTelemetry Protocol and how these traces can be collected and routed. It details tracing specifics for components like the kube-apiserver and kubelet.

This document explains how the Kubernetes TTL-after-finished controller manages the lifetime of finished Job objects. It details how to use the `.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` field to automatically clean up completed or failed Jobs.

This document explains Kubernetes volume populators and data sources, detailing how they pre-populate PersistentVolumeClaims with existing data. It covers the mechanisms for using custom populators and the differences between data source fields.

This document provides an introduction to how Kubernetes implements and controls API access. It references various documentation sections covering authentication, authorization methods, and service accounts.
This document defines an annotation as a key-value pair used to attach arbitrary, non-identifying metadata to objects. It explains that this metadata can be small, large, structured, or unstructured.

This document defines the role of an Application Architect, who is responsible for the high-level design of an application. The architect ensures the implementation allows for scalable and maintainable interaction with surrounding components.

The Container Device Interface (CDI) is a specification defining how devices are configured inside containers. Kubernetes uses CDI with device plugins and Dynamic Resource Allocation to provide device setup like bind mounts or environment variables to workloads.

This document outlines the terms under which a contributor grants a license to an open source project for their contributions. CLAs are used to resolve legal disputes regarding contributed material and intellectual property.

This document defines the role of a Cluster Operator, which is responsible for configuring, controlling, and monitoring clusters. Their main duty is ensuring the cluster remains operational through maintenance and upgrades.

This document explains what a condition is within Kubernetes resources. Conditions are fields in a resource's status that communicate the current state of that resource to other Kubernetes components.

containerd is a container runtime designed for simplicity, robustness, and portability. It functions as a daemon to handle tasks like fetching images, executing containers, and managing network access.

The Container Storage Interface (CSI) defines a standard interface for exposing storage systems to containers. It allows vendors to create custom storage plugins for Kubernetes as out-of-tree plugins.

This document defines what a 'Device' is within the system. It describes devices as infrastructure resources attached to nodes, such as GPUs or custom hardware, which require drivers for Kubernetes Pods to access them.
Dockershim is a component in Kubernetes versions up to 1.23 that enabled the kubelet to communicate with the Docker Engine. It has been removed in Kubernetes version 1.24 and later.
This document explains how duration values are represented in Kubernetes APIs. It details the format using non-negative integers combined with time unit suffixes.
An ephemeral container is a container type that can be temporarily run inside a pod for diagnostics. These containers lack resource guarantees and should not be used to run the main workload.

Extensions are software components that deeply integrate with Kubernetes to support new types of hardware. Most users benefit from pre-installed extensions in hosted or distribution Kubernetes clusters.

Group Version Resources (GVRs) are used to uniquely represent specific Kubernetes APIs by specifying the API group, version, and resource name. They ensure a stable way to access Kubernetes objects even when APIs evolve.

This document defines what a container image is, explaining that it is a stored instance of software needed to run an application. It describes how images are packaged for storage, pulling, and execution.

Istio is an open platform that provides a uniform way to integrate microservices, manage traffic, enforce policies, and aggregate telemetry. It acts as an infrastructure layer, often forming a service mesh, without requiring changes to application code.

This document describes how to authenticate and authorize access to the kubelet's HTTPS endpoint. It details methods like anonymous access control, X509 client certificate authentication, and bearer token usage.

This document describes the Kubelet Pods API, which allows node-local components to query information about Pods directly from the kubelet. It details the available gRPC operations and the underlying protobuf definitions.
This document specifies the format for a Kubernetes API object using JSON or YAML. A manifest defines the desired state of an object that Kubernetes will maintain.
This document explains the convention for naming objects within a resource, specifically detailing how client-provided strings refer to objects using URLs.

This document explains the various fields that constitute a Kubernetes Node's status, including addresses, conditions, capacity, info, and declared features. It details what each status field represents for cluster health monitoring.
This document describes a Persistent Volume (PV), which is an API object representing a piece of storage in the cluster. It explains how PVs abstract storage details for consumption.
Pod Priority defines the importance of a pod relative to others in a cluster. It allows users to set a scheduling priority for pods to control their placement and preemption.
This document details the TCP and UDP ports and protocols used by Kubernetes components in both the control plane and worker nodes. It specifies the purpose and usage of these network endpoints.

This document explains what a proxy server is and how it functions as an intermediary between a client and a remote service. It also mentions kube-proxy as a specific network proxy within a Kubernetes cluster.
This document explains what a replica is in Kubernetes, defining it as a copy of a Pod or set of Pods. It details how replicas are used to ensure high availability, scalability, and fault tolerance.
This document defines a template used by Kubernetes to create ResourceClaims. These templates enable dynamic resource allocation by providing per-Pod or per-PodGroup access to similar resources.

This document explains what a ServiceAccount is and its role in providing identity for processes running inside a Pod. It details how processes authenticate to the cluster using a specific service account.
Sidecar containers are containers started before main application containers that provide a Pod-local service to the main app. They continue running after the Pod starts, unlike init containers.

This document explains declarative admission policies in Kubernetes, detailing Validating and Mutating policies, their structure, and the use of Common Expression Language (CEL). It covers how policies enforce constraints or modify resources during admission.

This document explains how to load AppArmor profiles on nodes and enforce them in Pods to restrict container access to resources. It details prerequisites like kernel module support and container runtime compatibility.
This document introduces StatefulSets for managing stateful applications on Kubernetes. It demonstrates how to create, delete, scale, and update the Pods managed by a StatefulSet.
This document provides a tutorial on deploying a canary release in Kubernetes. It explains the steps to deploy a stable version, a canary version, route traffic, monitor, and complete the rollout.

This document provides a tutorial on how to deploy Apache Cassandra on Kubernetes using a StatefulSet. It explains how StatefulSets manage stateful applications and how to configure Cassandra for cluster discovery.

This tutorial guides users on how to use Minikube to start a Kubernetes cluster on their local machine. It explains what Kubernetes and Minikube are and outlines the necessary steps to set up the environment.

This document provides a tutorial on how to enforce the `baseline` Pod Security Standard at the cluster level using Pod Security Admission. It details the steps required to install necessary tools and choose the appropriate standard.
This document explains the steps to configure a Kubernetes Pod to use a PersistentVolumeClaim for storage. It details creating a PersistentVolume, a PersistentVolumeClaim, and a Pod.

This document provides a real-world example of configuring Redis by using a Kubernetes ConfigMap. It details the steps to create the ConfigMap, deploy a Redis Pod, and verify that the configuration is correctly applied within the container.
This document explains the Kubernetes model for connecting containers, how to expose pods to the cluster, and how to create a Service to provide a stable access point for applications.
This document provides step-by-step instructions on how to create a Kubernetes Service object with the LoadBalancer type to expose an application running in multiple pods to an external IP address.

This document provides a tutorial on building and deploying a multi-tier web application using Kubernetes and Docker. It details the steps for setting up a Redis leader, followers, and the guestbook frontend.

This document provides a tutorial on how to run a sample application on Kubernetes using minikube. It guides the user through creating a cluster, checking its status, opening the dashboard, and deploying an application.

This document provides a tutorial on how to install Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) drivers in a cluster and use DRA APIs to allocate hardware devices to Pods. It outlines the steps for deploying drivers, claiming resources, and observing the state.

This document provides steps to install and configure `cri-o` and `kubelet` on a Linux system to run a standalone Kubernetes node. It covers system preparation, configuration swaps, and enabling necessary networking.
